---
title: "Prediction bias and prediction variance"
---

The earlier pages defined [estimator bias](../statistical-inference/estimator-bias.qmd), [estimator variance](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd), and their contribution to [mean squared error](../statistical-inference/mean-squared-error.qmd). Here the estimator is a fitted prediction at a specified predictor vector. The same decomposition concerns prediction bias and prediction variance across repeated training samples.

A linear reading-time model may miss curvature in the association among length, frequency, surprisal, and mean response. A more flexible model may instead follow sample-specific variation. The [**bias-variance decomposition**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) separates these two failure modes.

## Beginning with repeated training samples

At a fixed predictor vector $x$, let the response be generated by

$$
Y=f(x)+\varepsilon,
$$

where $f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ and

$$
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=\sigma^2.
$$

Repeatedly drawing a comparable training sample and applying the same complete fitting procedure produces a different $\widehat f(x)$ on each repetition. Prediction variance describes variation among those learned predictions. It does not describe variation among observed responses with the same predictors.

The bias and prediction variance are

$$
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))
=
\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]-f(x)
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)]
=
\mathbb{E}\left[
  \left(\widehat f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]\right)^2
\right].
$$

## Deriving the decomposition

We want expected squared error for a new response at the fixed predictor vector:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\widehat f(x))^2\right].
$$

Add and subtract both $f(x)$ and $\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]$:

$$
Y-\widehat f(x)
=
\underbrace{Y-f(x)}_{\text{response noise}}
+
\underbrace{f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]}_{\text{negative bias}}
+
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\widehat f(x)]-\widehat f(x)}_{\text{training-sample variation}}.
$$

After squaring, the expected cross-products are zero because the response noise has mean zero and the fitted predictions are centered around their own expectation. Thus,

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\widehat f(x))^2\right]
=
\sigma^2
+
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))^2
+
\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)].
$$

The first term is **irreducible error** under the declared data-generating process. The other two terms depend on the complete learning procedure.

## An empirically calibrated Natural Stories simulation

True bias is not identified from one observed corpus. We thus use the only simulation in this module and label its assumptions. The code loads the [Natural Stories data](prediction-targets.qmd#natural-stories), averages responses and predictors to observed story positions, fits a cubic reference surface, and declares that fitted surface to be the simulation truth. Each repetition samples actual positions with replacement and adds a residual resampled from that empirical fit.

The target is also an observed position rather than an invented predictor vector. It is the position closest to the observed 90th percentile of surprisal and the median frequency and length.

```{r}
#| label: natural-bias-variance
#| message: false
#| warning: false

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
keep <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)
natural <- natural_all[keep, c(
  "story_id", "word_position", "log_rt", "word_length",
  "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)]
natural$position_id <- paste(
  natural$story_id, natural$word_position, sep = ":"
)

position_means <- aggregate(
  natural[c(
    "log_rt", "word_length", "log_unigram_frequency",
    "gpt3_surprisal"
  )],
  list(position_id = natural$position_id),
  mean
)
predictors <- c(
  "word_length", "log_unigram_frequency", "gpt3_surprisal"
)
position_center <- vapply(position_means[predictors], mean, numeric(1))
position_scale <- vapply(position_means[predictors], sd, numeric(1))
for (predictor in predictors) {
  position_means[[paste0(predictor, "_z")]] <-
    (position_means[[predictor]] - position_center[[predictor]]) /
    position_scale[[predictor]]
}

linear_formula <-
  log_rt ~ word_length_z + log_unigram_frequency_z + gpt3_surprisal_z
cubic_formula <-
  log_rt ~ word_length_z + I(word_length_z^2) + I(word_length_z^3) +
    log_unigram_frequency_z + I(log_unigram_frequency_z^2) +
    I(log_unigram_frequency_z^3) + gpt3_surprisal_z +
    I(gpt3_surprisal_z^2) + I(gpt3_surprisal_z^3)

reference_fit <- lm(cubic_formula, data = position_means)
reference_residuals <- residuals(reference_fit)

target_distance <- with(
  position_means,
  (gpt3_surprisal - quantile(gpt3_surprisal, 0.90))^2 /
      var(gpt3_surprisal) +
    (log_unigram_frequency - median(log_unigram_frequency))^2 /
      var(log_unigram_frequency) +
    (word_length - median(word_length))^2 / var(word_length)
)
target_position <- position_means[which.min(target_distance), ]
truth_at_target <- as.numeric(predict(reference_fit, target_position))

set.seed(20261103)
n_repetitions <- 300L
training_positions <- 400L
prediction_rows <- vector("list", n_repetitions * 2L)

for (repetition in seq_len(n_repetitions)) {
  sampled <- sample.int(
    nrow(position_means), training_positions, replace = TRUE
  )
  training <- position_means[sampled, ]
  training$log_rt <- as.numeric(predict(reference_fit, training)) +
    sample(reference_residuals, training_positions, replace = TRUE)

  linear_fit <- lm(linear_formula, data = training)
  cubic_fit <- lm(cubic_formula, data = training)
  prediction_rows[[2L * repetition - 1L]] <- data.frame(
    repetition = repetition,
    procedure = "Linear",
    prediction = as.numeric(predict(linear_fit, target_position))
  )
  prediction_rows[[2L * repetition]] <- data.frame(
    repetition = repetition,
    procedure = "Cubic",
    prediction = as.numeric(predict(cubic_fit, target_position))
  )
}

simulation_predictions <- do.call(rbind, prediction_rows)
irreducible_variance <- mean(reference_residuals^2)
bias_variance <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(simulation_predictions$prediction,
        simulation_predictions$procedure),
  function(values) {
    bias <- mean(values) - truth_at_target
    prediction_variance <- mean((values - mean(values))^2)
    data.frame(
      prediction_mean = mean(values),
      bias = bias,
      bias_squared = bias^2,
      prediction_variance = prediction_variance,
      irreducible_variance = irreducible_variance,
      expected_squared_error =
        bias^2 + prediction_variance + irreducible_variance
    )
  }
))
bias_variance$procedure <- rownames(bias_variance)
rownames(bias_variance) <- NULL
bias_variance

ggplot2::ggplot(
  simulation_predictions,
  ggplot2::aes(procedure, prediction)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_violin(
    fill = "grey88", color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.4, width = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = bias_variance,
    ggplot2::aes(procedure, prediction_mean),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2,
    color = "#2B6CB0"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(
    yintercept = truth_at_target,
    color = "grey25",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Learning procedure",
    y = "Predicted mean log reading time"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

At observed position `r target_position$position_id`, the declared mean is `r sprintf("%.5f", truth_at_target)` and the residual variance is `r sprintf("%.6f", irreducible_variance)`. The cubic procedure has squared bias `r sprintf("%.6f", bias_variance$bias_squared[bias_variance$procedure == "Cubic"])` and prediction variance `r sprintf("%.6f", bias_variance$prediction_variance[bias_variance$procedure == "Cubic"])`. The linear procedure has squared bias `r sprintf("%.6f", bias_variance$bias_squared[bias_variance$procedure == "Linear"])` and variance `r sprintf("%.6f", bias_variance$prediction_variance[bias_variance$procedure == "Linear"])`.

The flexible procedure reduces squared bias but increases prediction variance. Under this declared simulation, its expected squared error is `r sprintf("%.6f", bias_variance$expected_squared_error[bias_variance$procedure == "Cubic"])`, compared with `r sprintf("%.6f", bias_variance$expected_squared_error[bias_variance$procedure == "Linear"])` for the linear procedure. The gray violins show all repeated predictions, the blue points show their means, and the horizontal line shows the assumed truth.

## What the simulation establishes

This calibration demonstrates the decomposition using observed predictor values, response scale, and residuals. It does not estimate the unknown Natural Stories data-generating process. The cubic reference surface is assumed true for the exercise; another calibrated truth could change the comparison.

The example also shows why coefficient count is not a definition of prediction variance. Regularization, sample size, preprocessing, and the predictor distribution all affect how much a procedure changes across training samples. Held-out loss can evaluate their combined consequence, but it cannot identify separate bias and variance terms without an assumption about $f(x)$.

## Checking the decomposition

1. Across which repetitions is $\operatorname{Var}[\widehat f(x)]$ defined?
2. Which procedure has smaller squared bias at the selected Natural Stories position?
3. Which procedure has smaller expected squared error under the declared simulation?
4. Why is the horizontal line an assumed truth rather than an estimate of the unknown response process?

The bias-variance decomposition explains why a procedure that follows training data more closely need not predict a new response better. The [previous page](predictive-loss.qmd) defined held-out loss. The [next page](cross-validation.qmd) rotates the training and test roles to obtain predictions for every retained response.
